{{Punjabis}}

'''Lahnda''' ({{langx|pa|Laehndā}}, {{IPA|pa|lɛ˦n.d̪äː|pron}}, {{lit|western}}), also known as '''Western Punjabi''', is a proposed grouping of northwestern [[Indo-Aryan languages|Indo-Aryan]] [[variety (linguistics)|language varieties]] spoken primarily in [[Punjab, Pakistan|Punjab]], and most of [[Azad Kashmir]] in [[Pakistan]].{{efn|[[Shahmukhi]]: {{nq|لہندا}}, [[Gurmukhi]]: ਲਹਿੰਦਾ}} The term was introduced into linguistic literature by [[George Abraham Grierson]] during the compilation of the ''[[Linguistic Survey of India]]'' in the early 20th century.<ref name="Bailey1921" />

The classification traditionally includes varieties such as [[Saraiki language|Saraiki]], [[Hindko]], [[Pahari-Pothwari]], and several transitional Punjabi dialects.<ref name="Masica1991" /><ref name="Shackle1979" /> The term ''Lahnda'' is primarily an academic exonym and is generally not used by native speakers as a collective linguistic identity.<ref name="Masica1991" />

Modern comparative linguistics has questioned the validity of Lahnda as a coherent genetic subgroup within the Indo-Aryan language family.<ref name="Kogan2017" /><ref name="Masica1991" /> Several linguists describe the grouping as a classificatory convenience rather than a historically unified linguistic branch.<ref name="Masica1991" /> Contemporary scholarship often instead treats these varieties as forming part of a broader Northwestern Indo-Aryan or Punjabi dialect continuum.<ref name="Kogan2017" /><ref name="Shackle1980" />

The classification continues to appear in some linguistic literature and in the [[ISO 639]] standard, where Lahnda is assigned the macrolanguage code {{mono|lah}}.<ref>{{e26|lah}}</ref>

== Background ==

During the late 19th and early 20th centuries, British colonial linguists sought to classify the languages of the Indian subcontinent into genealogical categories. In the ''Linguistic Survey of India'', Grierson grouped several northwestern Punjabi varieties under the umbrella term ''Lahnda''.<ref name="Bailey1921" />

Grierson’s classification was influenced by the "Inner–Outer" hypothesis proposed by linguist [[August Friedrich Rudolf Hoernlé]], which divided Indo-Aryan languages into hypothetical "Inner" and "Outer" branches based on geographical and morphological criteria.<ref name="Kogan2017" /> Under this framework, Western Punjabi varieties were placed within the broader "Outer" Indo-Aryan category alongside languages such as [[Sindhi language|Sindhi]] and [[Bengali language|Bengali]].<ref name="Kogan2017" />

Later developments in comparative linguistics and historical phonology weakened support for the Inner–Outer model, which is no longer widely accepted in modern Indo-Aryan scholarship.<ref name="Kogan2017" />

== Scholarly debate ==

=== Criticism of the classification ===

A number of linguists have questioned whether Lahnda constitutes a valid genealogical subgroup within Indo-Aryan.<ref name="Masica1991" /><ref name="Kogan2017" /> Colin P. Masica described the grouping as problematic and noted uncertainty regarding its linguistic validity.<ref name="Masica1991" />

The classification has also been criticized because the varieties grouped under Lahnda often exhibit strong transitional relationships with neighbouring Punjabi dialects and lack a unified literary or ethnolinguistic identity.<ref name="Masica1991" />

=== Reassessment of the Inner–Outer hypothesis ===

The foundations of Grierson’s classification were challenged during the 20th century. Linguist [[Suniti Kumar Chatterji]] criticized the genealogical assumptions underlying the Inner–Outer hypothesis, arguing that many of its defining features represented areal or typological similarities rather than evidence of common descent.<ref name="Kogan2017" />

Modern lexicostatistical and comparative studies have similarly questioned the treatment of Lahnda as a separate genetic subgroup.<ref name="Kogan2017" /> Anton I. Kogan notes that Grierson’s classification relied heavily on typological observations rather than systematic comparative-historical reconstruction.<ref name="Kogan2017" />

=== Transitional character of the varieties ===

Scholars studying northwestern Indo-Aryan varieties have frequently emphasized their transitional nature. In his work on [[Hindko]], Christopher Shackle highlighted the gradual linguistic transition between Punjabi, Hindko, and neighbouring speech forms rather than sharply defined linguistic boundaries.<ref name="Shackle1980" />

Many linguists therefore describe the region as part of a broader Northwestern Indo-Aryan dialect continuum, in which linguistic features transition gradually across geographical areas.<ref name="Masica1991" /><ref name="Kogan2017" />

== Modern usage ==

Although the term has declined in common linguistic usage, ''Lahnda'' continues to appear in some academic works and language catalogues:

* as an [[ISO 639]] macrolanguage code ({{mono|lah}});
* in historical discussions of Grierson’s classification;
* and occasionally as a cover term for northwestern Punjabi varieties.

Contemporary scholarship more commonly refers to the individual language varieties by their specific names, such as [[Saraiki language|Saraiki]], [[Hindko]], [[Pahari-Pothwari]], or [[Punjabi language|Punjabi]].<ref name="Masica1991" />

==Name==
''Lahnda'' means "western" in Punjabi. It was coined by [[William St. Clair Tisdall]] (in the form ''Lahindā'') probably around 1890 and later adopted by a number of linguists — notably [[George Abraham Grierson]] — for a dialect group that had no general local name.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Grierson|first=George A.|year=1930|title=Lahndā and Lahndī|journal=Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies|volume=5|issue=4|pages=883–887|doi=10.1017/S0041977X00090571|s2cid=160784067 }}</ref>{{rp|883}} This term has currency only among linguists.{{sfn|Masica|1991|p=18}}

==Development==
[[Fariduddin Ganjshakar|Baba Farid]] (c. 1188–1266), a celebrated and revered Punjabi Sufi saint of the 12th century, composed poetry in the Lahnda lect.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Johar |first=Surinder Singh |title=Guru Gobind Singh : a multi-faceted personality |date=1999 |publisher=M.D. Publications |isbn=81-7533-093-7 |location=New Delhi |pages=56 |oclc=52865201}}</ref>

[[Mian Muhammad Bakhsh]] (c. 1830 – 1907) is another Punjabi poet who composed poetry in a mixture of both the Eastern and Lahnda varieties of Punjabi.<ref>{{Cite web |date=22 March 2019 |title=Mian Muhammad Bakhsh – A great Punjabi Sufi Poet |url=https://nation.com.pk/30-Aug-2017/mian-muhammad-bakhsh-a-great-punjabi-sufi-poet |access-date=3 May 2023 |archive-date=22 March 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190322044412/https://nation.com.pk/30-Aug-2017/mian-muhammad-bakhsh-a-great-punjabi-sufi-poet |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref>

[[Saraiki language|Saraiki]] (in the south) and [[Hindko]] (in the northwest) have been cultivated as literary standards.<ref name="Shackle 2010">{{cite book|last=Shackle|first=Christopher|author-link=Christopher Shackle|chapter=Lahnda|page=635|year=2010|editor1-last=Brown|editor1-first=Keith|editor2-last=Ogilvie|editor2-first=Sarah|title=Concise Encyclopedia of Languages of the World|location=Oxford|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=9780080877754}}</ref> The development of the standard written Saraiki began in the 1960s.{{sfn|Rahman|1997|p=838}}{{sfn|Shackle|1977}} The national census of Pakistan has counted Saraiki speakers since 1981, and Hindko speakers from 2017, prior to which both were represented by Punjabi in general.{{sfn|Javaid|2004|p=46}}

==Classification==
Lahnda has several traits that distinguish it from other Punjabi linguistic groups, such as a future tense in ''-s-''. Like [[Sindhi language|Sindhi]], Saraiki retains breathy-voiced consonants, has developed implosives, and lacks tone. Hindko, also called ''Panjistani'' or (ambiguously) ''Pahari'', is more like [[Majhi dialect|Central Punjabi]] in this regard, though the equivalent of the low-rising tone of Central Punjabi is a high-falling tone in Peshawar Hindko.<ref name="Shackle 2010" />
[[File:Linguistic map of India, showing the areas where Indo-Aryan languages are spoken, published in the 'Imperial Gazetteer of India' (Vol. XXVI, Atlas; 1931 revised edition; plate no. 13).jpg|thumb|Lahnda depicted on a linguistic map of India, showing the areas where Indo-Aryan languages are spoken, published in the 'Imperial Gazetteer of India' (Vol. XXVI, Atlas; 1931 revised edition; plate no. 13).]]
Sindhi and Punjabi groups (including Lahnda) form a [[dialect continuum]] with no clear-cut boundaries. ''[[Ethnologue]]'' classifies the western forms of Central Punjabi and the dialects transitional between Lahnda and Central Punjabi as Lahnda, so that the Lahnda–Eastern Punjabi isogloss approximates the Pakistani–Indian border.<ref>{{e18|lah}}</ref>

== Script ==
Lahndi-speaking [[Sikhs]] employ the [[Gurmukhi]] script for recording the language rather than the Perso-Arabic-based [[Shahmukhi]] script.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Smirnov |first=Yuri Andreyevich |title=The Lahndi Language |publisher=Nauka Publishing House, Central Department of Oriental Literature |year=1975 |pages=28 |quote=Lahndi-speaking Sikhs frequently use the Gurmukhi alphabet to write texts in the language.}}</ref>
